title: Who is my neighbor? (Luke 10:25–37)
hook: a lawyer's question and a story that asks who acted like a neighbor

segments.voice: Yesterday, nepioi: what the clever missed, revealed to little children. Your line was revealed to babes.

It starts as a test. A lawyer, an expert in the law of Moses, stands up: "Master, what shall I do to inherit eternal life?" Jesus turns it back: how do you read the law? The lawyer answers well, joining two lines from Deuteronomy and Leviticus: "Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy strength, and with all thy mind; and thy neighbour as thyself." Jesus says: "This do, and thou shalt live." But the lawyer, wanting to justify himself, asks one more question, about where the edges are.

"And who is my neighbour?" Where can I stop? Jesus answers with a story. "A certain man went down from Jerusalem to Jericho, and fell among thieves, which stripped him of his raiment, and wounded him, and departed, leaving him half dead." A priest passes by on the other side. Then a Levite, a temple worker, does the same. Readers have guessed why, fear, hurry, worry about touching what might be a corpse, but Luke is silent. Then a Samaritan comes, one of the same people whose village, a chapter ago, would not receive Jesus. "And when he saw him, he had compassion on him," the same words Luke used for Jesus at the widow's gate in Nain. He bandages the wounds, pouring in oil and wine, puts the man on his own animal and walks. He leaves two coins, two pence in the King James, with the innkeeper: "Take care of him; and whatsoever thou spendest more, when I come again, I will repay thee." Then Jesus flips the question: "Which now of these three, thinkest thou, was neighbour unto him that fell among the thieves?" The lawyer doesn't say the word Samaritan; some readers think he couldn't bring himself to. He says: "He that shewed mercy on him." And Jesus: "Go, and do thou likewise." The lawyer wanted a boundary. He gets a verb. Neighbor isn't a category of people you owe. It's something you become.
screen: `WHO IS MY NEIGHBOR? WHERE DO I STOP?`
`A PRIEST, A LEVITE: THE OTHER SIDE.`
`NOT WHO IS, BUT WHO WAS A NEIGHBOR.`
then, large: `GO, AND DO THOU LIKEWISE.`

segments.voice: Think about your own road, the commute, the hallway at work, the group chat, and who has been left out, knocked down by bad news, or stuck beside it. Then think of someone from the other side of some line, politics, faith, class, a family feud, hold them in mind without arguing, and picture crossing the road toward them as the Samaritan did, with one small act of mercy. If you pray, hold that person before God; if you don't, simply picture the crossing.
Plesion, the Greek word behind neighbor, meaning the one near you: a lawyer's question, and Jesus' story of a Samaritan who stops on the road, turning the question into who acted as a neighbor.
Your line: go and do likewise. Mercy crossed the road. That's day five hundred forty-one.

howItsDone: Hospitals, charities and the emergency-helper laws known as Good Samaritan laws take their name from this story.

original.note: Greek: near, nearby, the one near you. the word behind "neighbor."

trapdoor: what you thought: be nice to strangers.
what it means: the lawyer asks who counts as his neighbor, and Jesus turns it into who acted as one. neighbor becomes a verb.
what a scholar hears: "neighbor" is plesion, the one near. Jesus' question moves it from who is near me to whom I draw near to.
recall: to heal and to save, one word

chat.says: So who counts as my neighbor, according to the good Samaritan story?
options: Jesus flips it: not who counts, but who acted as a neighbor. Go and do likewise.
Only the people who live right next door; that's what the word means.
Only people who have helped you first; mercy is something you pay back.
chat.meaning: Jesus turns the lawyer's question around: which of these three was neighbor to the man? Neighbor isn't a category; it's something you become.

Samaritan.meaning: someone from Samaria, like the village that refused Jesus

Jericho.meaning: the town at the end of the road from Jerusalem

Nain.meaning: the town where Jesus had compassion on a grieving widow

Deuteronomy.meaning: a book of the law of Moses

notes: The priest and Levite: the script says the text is silent on their reasons and lists common guesses without endorsing one, so as not to make temple workers or Jewish law the foil. Keeper to confirm.
'Two coins, roughly two days' wages' assumes a denarius as a day's wage (Matthew 20:2). Confirm.

Reviewer edit: 'The lawyer can't quite bring himself to say the word Samaritan' was stated as fact; now 'the lawyer doesn't say the word Samaritan; many readers think he couldn't bring himself to.' Confirm.
Samaritan-Jewish hostility described as mutual and historical.
'Laws that protect people who help' refers to Good Samaritan laws in many places. General.
